sparkberry.title: Sparkberry
sparkberry.subtitle: AI-Powered Catbot
sparkberry.description: A compact 3D-printed AI catbot designed to bring an AI personality into the physical world.

mainImage.caption: Fig 2.1: Schematic of the final Sparkberry version.

secondaryImage.caption: Fig 2.2: 3D CAD visualization of the chassis geometry. The design is simple, and actually the simplest way to fit the electronics and motors into a small, cat-like shape: a box with dedicated compartments for microphone, battery and display.

sections.title: A Cat-Sized Interface for AI
sections.content: SparkBerry is a small interactive robot designed to bring an AI personality into the physical world. Built as a small geometric cat, it combines a two-wheel platform with expressive eyes and a microphone for natural interaction. The result is a desk companion that does not simply answer requests: it reacts, moves, looks around, gets sleepy, and makes the invisible logic of an AI system feel tangible.

sections.title: More Than a Desk Toy
sections.content: The project was conceived as an autonomous bridge between software intelligence and physical behavior. Its ESP32 handles the real-time work that must remain immediate and reliable—motor control, display animation, audio sampling, and WebSocket communication—while the heavier language processing runs remotely through a Raspberry Pi 5 AI core. This separation keeps the robot responsive without sacrificing the flexibility of a conversational model.

sections.title: The Mechanical Design
sections.content: SparkBerry's body is a modular 3D-printed enclosure developed around the constraints of its electronics. The base accommodates the dual 18650 battery holder and the microphone other than a stepdown converter; the two classic yellow TT gear motors are at the base, while the upper shell protects the ESP32 keep restrained around 25 jumper cables necessary to connect to the various components. The front display gives the robot a recognizable face without adding unnecessary mechanical complexity. Designing around real cable clearances, and serviceability turned the chassis into an engineering problem rather than a decorative shell.

sections.title: A Face Made of Pixels
sections.content: The 128x128 OLED is the emotional center of SparkBerry. Instead of relying on a camera or a collection of moving parts, the robot communicates through animated eyes and simple visual states. It can blink, sleep, look left or right, and express happiness, curiosity, dizziness, anger, or excitement. A technical debug mode can also expose Wi-Fi information, signal strength, IP address, microphone volume, and the current emotion, making the small display useful during development as well as during normal interaction.

sections.title: Movement with Personality
sections.content: The two motor-driven wheels give SparkBerry a compact differential-drive platform capable of moving forward and backward, turning in place, and executing short choreographed sequences. The command registry maps high-level intentions such as approach, spin, look around, dance, and anger into timed motion and expression combinations. A simple request can therefore become a complete physical reaction: the robot can move independently and change its eyes as one coordinated action.

sections.title: Listening Locally
sections.content: An INMP441 digital microphone feeds audio to the ESP32 through I2S, where volume and activity are monitored continuously. Recognized speech is handled by a local Vosk-based STT service, with a constrained vocabulary for common commands and a fallback to open-vocabulary recognition. Frequently used triggers are matched locally first for near-instant responses: calling SparkBerry closer, asking it to spin or dance, telling it to sleep, or switching between animated eyes and technical text does not require waiting for the language model.

sections.title: The AI Connection
sections.content: When a phrase is not a direct local trigger, the backend forwards it to its backend via a secure tunnel, a Raspberry Pi 5 AI core of its ecosystem. Turberry is instructed to interpret the user's intent and return a strict JSON command containing both an action and the catbot's speech. The backend validates that action against the command registry, translates it into movement and emotion, and safely falls back to a happy idle state if the model is unavailable, times out after a few seconds, or returns an invalid response. This keeps the personality expressive while ensuring that unreliable network or AI behavior cannot leave the robot in an undefined state.

sections.title: A Robot That Knows When to Rest
sections.content: SparkBerry includes a small but deliberate layer of autonomy. After five minutes without meaningful sound or interaction, it enters an animated sleeping state with closed, breathing eyes. A new sound above the configured threshold or a voice command wakes it again, with a short cooldown to avoid accidental oscillation. The sleep behavior makes the robot feel less like a device that is always waiting and more like a companion with its own quiet rhythm.

sections.title: A Personal Experiment in Embodied AI
sections.content: SparkBerry brings together embedded C++, a Node.js WebSocket backend, local speech recognition, remote language models, and parametric 3D design in one small platform. Its value is not only in the individual features, but in the way they reinforce one another: software commands become motion, language becomes expression, and a tiny printed chassis becomes a physical endpoint for an entire self-hosted AI ecosystem.

cameraberry.title: Cameraberry 3
cameraberry.subtitle: A MODERN DIY RETRO CAMERA
cameraberry.description: A modern retro camera, fully designed and built from the ground up as a solo endeavor.

mainImage.caption: Fig 1.1: Schematic of the final Cameraberry 3 version.

secondaryImage.caption: Fig 1.2: 3D CAD visualization of the chassis geometry.

sections.title: A Statement of Personality
sections.content: In an era of mass-produced, powerful, and ready-to-use imaging devices, the Cameraberry project emerges as a statement of technical personality. Entirely conceived and built as a solo endeavor, this project was born from the desire to bridge the gap between digital code and physical reality. It served as a personal playground to experiment with a diverse tech stack while working directly with the hardware, demonstrating that sophisticated tools can be built from the ground up with enough curiosity and persistent debugging.

sections.title: Beyond a Simple Camera
sections.content: The Cameraberry 3 is not merely a camera; it is a surprisingly powerful computer designed for deep experimentation, merged with the soul of an instant camera. Utilizing a custom-designed chassis and incorporating a thermal printer, it bridges the gap between raw hardware components and sophisticated software capabilities.

sections.title: The Design Process
sections.content: The physical form of the Cameraberry 3 was no easy feat. The chassis design required countless iterations and precise measurements of every internal component. After initial, cumbersome attempts with Fusion360, I found my stride by switching to OpenSCAD. By pairing code-based modeling with the power of LLM-assisted code, I was able to programmatically define the geometry and refine the case until it met the project's rugged, functional requirements.

sections.title: Technical Backbone
sections.content: The schematic reveals a compact, rugged design. Key features include physical controls for manual interaction—a nod to the tactile nature of classic photography—integrated with a modern digital backbone. The system is connected to a self-hosted backend, enabling LLM-powered image descriptions and n8n-powered workflows for on-the-go image and prompt manipulation. Additionally, a dedicated service hosts a YOLO instance for real-time object recognition, while a remote web server allows for wireless capture and full control.

sections.title: The Backend Ecosystem
sections.content: The dedicated backend infrastructure deserves a special mention: it is powered by two additional Raspberry Pi 5 boards. One functions as a secure internet gateway, hosting the web server and remote control services plus an n8n instance, while the second is overclocked to 3GHz to handle demanding LLM and YOLO processes—all seamlessly and securely integrated into a unified ecosystem.

sections.title: Intelligent Processing
sections.content: The backend provides two distinct processing modes: a 'fast' mode that delivers abstract, poetic descriptions in just 15 seconds—using YOLO object detection to feed the LLM prompt and bypass full image inference time—and a 'detailed' mode that generates comprehensive analysis by processing the entire image through the LLM within about a minute. These processes run in parallel with the printing phase for near-instant feedback. Through the n8n-powered workflow, the system can also archive the original high-resolution image for further processing or instant mobile notifications. Of course, the camera remains fully functional for traditional offline shooting whenever needed.

sections.title: A Personal Milestone
sections.content: This project is a milestone in my personal research into hardware-software integration, demonstrating that sophisticated tools can be built from the ground up with enough curiosity and persistent debugging.

gallery.desc: The original prototype. This early version lacked a display and a physical power button, making safe shutdowns impossible without disconnecting the power supply. The initial 'tower' design was eventually abandoned in favor of a more usable form factor.

gallery.title: Evolution: v1 vs v2
gallery.desc: A comparison between the first and second iterations. The second version introduced status LEDs and a more refined design. The signature horizontal white band was a happy accident caused by running out of filament during printing, then intentionally kept for the following models.

gallery.desc: Internal view of the Cameraberry 2. This version laid the groundwork for the current iteration, with optimized component placement and a storage slot for backup thermal paper. The 'spaghetti' cable management system ensures a clean and organized interior. I promise.
